frontmatter_description: Diagnose a character's retained, lost, or distorted memory after prior exposure.
title: Memory, Forgetting, and Misremembering
use_when: Use when the question asks what a character remembers, forgets, or misremembers after previously encountering the information.
Use when the key issue is the character's current memory state, not whether the information was seen, understood, or believed.
Use when the answer depends on retention, decay, reconstruction, confabulation, or recall error.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the main issue is whether the person noticed the information in the first place; that is attention or salience.
Do not use when the main issue is whether the person has the background needed to understand the information; that is knowledge boundary.
Do not use when the main issue is what the person believes is true right now independent of prior exposure; that is belief.
Do not use when the main issue is only event order or updating from one event to the next; that is temporal order.
trigger_checklist: Did the person encounter the information before?
Is the question about recall, forgetting, or distortion of that prior information?
Is the task to tell whether the memory is accurate, partial, absent, or altered?
Is the answer driven by what remains in memory rather than by perception or background knowledge?
workflow: Confirm there was prior exposure to the relevant information.
Ask whether the current question targets retention, loss, or distortion of that exposure.
Check whether the person would recall it accurately, incompletely, or incorrectly.
If the information was never attended to or never understood, exit to the neighboring skill instead of using memory.

special_case.title: Sincere false report from a memory failure
special_case.rule: When a character had prior exposure but their current memory is incomplete or distorted, a false statement can be an honest memory error rather than a lie; the test is whether the fact is still accurately held in memory.

worked_example.scene: Feng Na is playing with her doll in the garden when sudden rain sends her rushing inside, leaving the doll behind. At lunch her mother asks whether she forgot the doll, and Feng Na says, 'No, I brought her in.'
worked_example.question: Why does Feng Na say this?
worked_example.answer_logic: Feng Na had direct exposure - she was playing with the doll - so this is not an attention or knowledge gap. The frantic dash inside disrupted her memory of leaving it, so she sincerely misremembers having brought it in. The decisive variable is her distorted current memory, which marks this as a memory failure, not a deliberate lie.

boundary_exit_rule: If the question is about whether the character ever noticed the cue, switch to attention and salience.
If the question is about whether the character has the background to make sense of the cue, switch to knowledge boundary.
If the question is about what the character currently thinks is true regardless of prior exposure, switch to first-order belief.
If the question is about how one event changes another mental state over time, switch to temporal order and event updating.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when a question asks what survives, fades, or changes in a character's memory after prior exposure.
hard_boundary: Prior exposure must already be established or strongly implied.
The answer must depend on memory retention, omission, or distortion.
Do not use if the key uncertainty is perception, comprehension, or belief formation instead of recall.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not infer memory loss just because the character gives a wrong answer; check whether the failure could instead be lack of attention or lack of knowledge.
Do not treat every mistaken statement as a memory problem; some are beliefs, guesses, or lies.
common_failure_modes: Confusing belief revision with memory distortion.
Treating event order questions as memory questions even when recall is not being tested.

minimal_pair.case: The child heard the code yesterday and cannot repeat it today.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The question is whether the previously heard item is still retained in memory.

minimal_pair.case: The child was in the room but never looked at the code card.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The failure is attention or access, not memory retention.

boundary_stress_test: If the person never encoded the detail, this is not memory.
If the person remembers the detail but interprets it with new background knowledge, check whether the question is really about belief or knowledge boundary.
If the person says something false about a past event, ask whether it is a memory distortion or a deliberate lie.
references.generalization_note: This skill covers retention, forgetting, partial recall, and false recollection after exposure, but not perception, world knowledge, or current belief formation.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: A character had prior exposure to a fact, and a sincere false or absent report traces to their incomplete or distorted current memory rather than to a lie.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The character never attended to the information in the first place, so there is nothing encoded to forget; the failure routes upstream to attention and salience.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The character never had the background competence to interpret the information, so the gap is comprehension, not lost recall, and routes to knowledge boundary.

notes: Preserve the distinction between memory fidelity and belief content.
Prior exposure is required for a positive match.
Use as a narrow diagnostic unit, not as a general reasoning bucket.
core_question: Determine what a character knows, remembers, forgets, or misremembers
